Dataset structure¶

What this project actually contains, and how the pieces fit together — the experimental design, the reference genomes, and the way a bacterial and a plant genome are combined into one index so that a single alignment pass can separate the two organisms.

This is the companion to 01_results_overview.ipynb, which covers what came out of the pipeline. Read this one first if you are new to the dataset.

# The Makefile is the single source of truth for which genome each sample uses,
# so parse it rather than restating the mapping here.
mk = (ROOT / "Makefile").read_text()
ACC     = dict(re.findall(r"^ACC_(\w+)\s*:?=\s*(\S+)", mk, re.M))
HOSTOF  = dict(re.findall(r"^HOST_([\w.-]+)\s*=\s*(\S+)", mk, re.M))
ANNOT   = re.search(r"^ANNOT_HOSTS\s*:?=\s*(.*)$", mk, re.M).group(1).split()
HOSTS   = re.search(r"^HOSTS\s*:?=\s*(.*)$", mk, re.M).group(1).split()

meta["ref_genome"] = meta.index.map(HOSTOF)
meta["strain_geno"] = meta["strain"] + " " + meta["genotype"]
pretty = lambda g: g.replace("_", " ").replace(" proxy", " (proxy)").capitalize()

pd.DataFrame({"accession": pd.Series(ACC), "annotated": pd.Series({h: h in ANNOT for h in HOSTS}),
              "samples": pd.Series({h: (meta.ref_genome == h).sum() for h in HOSTS})})

1. The experiment¶

Fourteen galls. Two Agrobacterium strains (1416 and 29), three genotypes — wild type plus two 1416 mutants, G-19 and G-30 — across seven host plantings, with gall ages spanning 26 to 635 days.

The design is a survey rather than a factorial: every cell below holds one gall, and most strain × host combinations were never sampled. Nothing here is replicated, so the figures in the results notebook describe individual libraries and cannot support a statistical contrast.

2. The reference genomes¶

Eight genomes are involved: two Agrobacterium strains and six plant assemblies. They differ enormously in size — a plant host genome is 50 to 160 times the bacterium — and only three of the six plants carry gene models.

Two substitutions are worth keeping in mind, both forced by what exists publicly:

  • Euonymus galls are aligned to E. europaeus (GCA_963580455.1), a congener, because there is no E. japonicus assembly.
  • Citrus (trifoliate) galls are counted on C. sinensis — Poncirus trifoliata has an assembly but no annotation. That genome was downloaded and indexed, then dropped from the run.
In [5]:
# Sizes come from the alignment indexes themselves (idxstats), so they describe
# exactly what was searched rather than what a datasheet claims.
host_size, agro_size = {}, {}
for s in meta.index:
    d = gv.load_idxstats(s)
    a, p = d[d.ref.str.startswith("agro_")], d[~d.ref.str.startswith("agro_")]
    host_size.setdefault(meta.loc[s, "ref_genome"], (p.length.sum(), len(p)))
    agro_size.setdefault(f"strain_{meta.loc[s, 'strain']}", (a.length.sum(), len(a)))

# Poncirus is in no index that was aligned against, so measure its FASTA directly.
pon = ROOT / "references/plant_host/poncirus_trifoliata/poncirus_trifoliata.fasta"
if "poncirus_trifoliata" not in host_size and pon.exists():
    L = n = 0
    with open(pon) as fh:
        for line in fh:
            if line.startswith(">"):
                n += 1
            else:
                L += len(line.strip())
    host_size["poncirus_trifoliata"] = (L, n)

def gene_count(gff):
    p = Path(gff)
    if not p.exists():
        return np.nan
    ids = {ln.split("ID=")[1].split(";")[0]
           for ln in p.read_text().splitlines() if "\tgene\t" in ln and "ID=" in ln}
    return len(ids)

rows = []
for k, (L, n) in agro_size.items():
    rows.append(dict(reference=k, kind="Agrobacterium", accession="collaborator assembly",
                     size_mb=L / 1e6, contigs=n,
                     genes=gene_count(ROOT / f"references/agrobacterium/{k}/{k}.gff3"),
                     samples=(("strain_" + meta.strain) == k).sum()))
for h in HOSTS:
    L, n = host_size.get(h, (np.nan, np.nan))
    rows.append(dict(reference=h, kind="plant host", accession=ACC.get(h, ""),
                     size_mb=L / 1e6, contigs=n,
                     genes=gene_count(ROOT / f"references/plant_host/{h}/{h}.gff3"),
                     samples=(meta.ref_genome == h).sum()))
refs = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("reference")
refs.round(2)

The bacterial side, to scale¶

Each Agrobacterium strain is five replicons: two chromosomes and three plasmids. The Ti plasmid is the smallest of them at about 0.2 Mb — 3 % of the genome — and carries the T-DNA, the segment that ends up transferred into the plant. That is where nearly all the "bacterial" signal in the results notebook turns out to sit.

    lens[st] = dict(zip(d.ref.str.rsplit("_", n=1).str[-1], d.length))

3. How the two genomes are combined¶

The pipeline does not align each sample twice. Instead it concatenates the bacterial and plant references into a single FASTA, builds one HISAT2 index from it, and aligns each sample once against that.

The reason is competitive assignment. With two separate alignments, a read from a conserved region could map acceptably to both genomes and be counted twice — once as plant, once as bacterium. With both genomes in one index, HISAT2 scores every read against all sequences at once and reports the best hit, so each read lands on one organism or neither.

Contig names carry the split: everything from the bacterium is prefixed agro_<strain>_, so the two organisms can be separated afterwards by name alone.

4. What the size difference implies¶

Because the host genome is 50–160× the bacterium, the bacterium is a very small target in every library. The chart below sets each sample's observed bacterial read share against the share of the combined reference that is bacterial.

The reference share is not a biological expectation — transcript abundance does not follow genome size, and a gall is mostly plant tissue with comparatively few bacterial cells. It is a scale marker: it shows that the observed bacterial fraction runs one to three orders of magnitude below even that crude line, which is what makes the bacterial matrices too shallow to use.

In [10]:

                          (agro_size[f"strain_{meta.loc[s, 'strain']}"][0] +
                           host_size[meta.loc[s, "ref_genome"]][0])

5. What exists at the end¶

Annotation availability, not sequencing, decides which galls end up with a usable expression matrix. Three of the six plant references carry gene models; the other three yield alignments and nothing countable.

6. Library preparation, read back out of the data¶

The repo documents a wet-lab protocol — 5 µg total RNA, Ribo-Zero rRNA Removal (Bacteria), TruSeq Stranded mRNA with the polyA-capture step skipped — but that section of README.md describes the 2019 reference paper, not these galls. How our own libraries were prepared is not recorded anywhere in the repo. It matters enormously, so the next best thing is to ask the reads.

Gene biotype composition is diagnostic. A library that skipped polyA capture and used a bacterial rRNA kit would leave plant rRNA completely undepleted, and plant rRNA would swamp everything. A polyA-selected library does the opposite: rRNA near zero, non-polyadenylated small RNAs absent, protein-coding dominant.

In [12]:
import re

BIOTYPE_GROUPS = ["protein_coding", "lncRNA", "rRNA", "other"]

def biotypes(host):
    out = {}
    for ln in open(ROOT / f"references/plant_host/{host}/{host}.gff3"):
        if "\tgene\t" not in ln:
            continue
        a = ln.split("\t")[8]
        i, b = re.search(r"ID=([^;]+)", a), re.search(r"gene_biotype=([^;\n]+)", a)
        if i and b:
            out[i.group(1)] = b.group(1) if b.group(1) in BIOTYPE_GROUPS else "other"
    return out

comp = {}
for p in sorted((ROOT / "04_matrix").glob("plant_*.tsv")):
    host = p.stem.replace("plant_", "")
    m = pd.read_csv(p, sep="\t", index_col=0)
    lookup = biotypes(host)                      # parse each GFF once, not once per gene
    bt = pd.Series({k: lookup.get(k, "other") for k in m.index})
    frac = 100 * m.groupby(bt).sum() / m.sum()
    for s in m.columns:
        comp[s] = frac[s].reindex(BIOTYPE_GROUPS).fillna(0)
comp = pd.DataFrame(comp).T
comp = comp.reindex([s for s in meta.index if s in comp.index])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.5, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
left = np.zeros(len(comp)); y = np.arange(len(comp))
for i, b in enumerate(BIOTYPE_GROUPS):
    ax.barh(y, comp[b], left=left, height=0.62, color=SERIES[i],
            edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=1.2, label=b.replace("_", " "))
    left += comp[b].values
ax.set_yticks(y, comp.index); ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_xlabel("% of counted reads")
ax.set_title("Counted reads by gene biotype")
clean(ax, "x")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, -0.16), ncols=4, borderaxespad=0)

ax = axes[1]
barh(ax, comp.index, comp["rRNA"], [SERIES[2]] * len(comp), "{:.2f}%")
ax.set_yticklabels([])
ax.set_title("rRNA share, enlarged")
ax.set_xlabel("% of counted reads")
note(ax, "A library that skipped polyA capture and depleted only bacterial rRNA would sit far off\n"
         "this scale — plant rRNA is untouched by a bacterial kit and would dominate the run.",
     y=-0.24)
plt.tight_layout(); save(fig, "27_library_composition"); plt.show()

A second, independent line: how much of the library is intronic¶

The biotype argument has one soft spot. Low rRNA in a count matrix can also arise from rRNA repeats collapsing in the assembly and their reads being thrown out as multi-mapping, so depletion is not strictly provable from gene classes alone.

Read position has no such escape hatch. A polyA library carries mature, spliced mRNA and is almost purely exonic; a ribo-depleted total-RNA library retains pre-mRNA and typically runs 20–40 % intronic.

Measuring it takes one extra step, because the pipeline counts with -t gene — introns sit inside the counted feature, so Unassigned_NoFeatures is intergenic only, and is not an intron measurement. scripts/intron_fraction.sh re-counts the same BAMs with -t exon, which pushes intronic reads out of the assigned pile:

intronic = NoFeatures(exon-level) − NoFeatures(gene-level)
In [13]:

intr["intergenic_pct"] = 100 * intr.intergenic / intr.located

What that means¶

Two independent measurements agree:

  • Gene class — rRNA is 0.3–3 % of counted reads, protein-coding is 95–98 %, and the non-polyadenylated small RNAs (snoRNA, snRNA, miRNA) are flat zero.
  • Read position — introns hold 1.0–2.1 % of located reads, an order of magnitude below what a ribo-depleted total-RNA library gives.

Both point one way: these are polyA-selected libraries. That is not the protocol written down in the repo.

The consequence runs through everything in the results notebook. Bacterial mRNA is not polyadenylated, so a polyA selection removes it by design. What survives on the Agrobacterium reference is the T-DNA: those genes sit in the plant genome after transfer, are transcribed by plant RNA polymerase II, and are polyadenylated like any other plant message — so they pass the selection while the bacterium's own chromosome does not.

That single fact explains the shape of the whole result: a bacterial fraction of 0.004–0.4 %, a silent chromosome, and all of the signal sitting in the T-DNA.

It also changes the recommendation. The bacterial transcriptome here is not under-sequenced, it is selected against — more depth on these libraries would return more plant mRNA and proportionally as little bacterium. Recovering it needs a different preparation: rRNA depletion without polyA capture, ideally with bacterial enrichment, as the 2019 protocol in the repo actually describes.

This is inference, not a kit name¶

Worth being exact about the standing of this claim, because a strong conclusion now rests on it. No record of the library preparation exists in the project. Not in the repo, not in README.md, and not in the vendor's own report: 30-1348328766/Azenta_30-1348328766_Data_Report.html gives customer, quote number and an Illumina 2x150bp configuration, and its Sample Type field is empty. There is no kit, prep or selection field anywhere in it.

So the polyA reading is an inference from two independent properties of the reads, and it should be labelled that way in any write-up. Settling it documentarily means the Azenta order behind quote 30-1348328766, or asking the submitting lab.

A third line of evidence is available and cheap: strandedness. The counts were produced with STRAND=0 because strandedness was never confirmed, and a TruSeq Stranded library would show a clear antisense asymmetry. Testing it would both corroborate the prep and settle whether the matrices should be rebuilt with -s 2 — an open question flagged in the Makefile header.

7. A spliced aligner over a bacterial genome¶

HISAT2 is built for eukaryotic transcriptomes: its purpose is to place reads across introns. Bacterial transcripts have none, so on the bacterial contigs that ability can only produce false joins. The pipeline runs

hisat2 -p $(THREADS) --dta -x references/combined/<strain>__<host> ...

with splicing enabled and no --no-spliced-alignment, and because a combined index means one set of flags for both organisms, the bacterium cannot be treated differently from the host without giving up the single competitive pass.

scripts/splice_rates.sh measures what that costs: how many alignments carry an N (skipped region) in their CIGAR, per organism.

In [14]:
sr = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "logs/splice_rates.tsv", sep="\t").set_index("sample")
sr = sr.reindex([s for s in meta.index if s in sr.index])
sr["agro_pct"] = 100 * sr.agro_spliced / sr.agro_alignments
sr["plant_pct"] = 100 * sr.plant_spliced / sr.plant_alignments

Splicing is doing real work on the plant side — 3 % to 40 % of alignments, depending on the species and the chromosome sampled — so it cannot simply be switched off. On the bacterial side it fires on 0 % to 3.3 % of alignments, which is noise rather than nothing: a spuriously spliced read spanning two genes lands in featureCounts' ambiguous bin rather than on either gene.

At that rate it cannot manufacture the T-DNA result, where single genes carry 43–66 % of a sample's bacterial counts. If the bacterial side ever carries real signal, the cheap fix is to drop N-CIGAR alignments on agro_* contigs before counting — it needs no re-alignment and keeps the competitive assignment that the combined index exists to provide.

In one paragraph¶

Fourteen unreplicated galls, each one strain on one host, are aligned against a reference built for that pairing: the strain's five replicons concatenated with the host assembly into a single HISAT2 index, bacterial contigs prefixed agro_. One alignment pass per sample assigns every read to its better match, and the prefix splits the result afterwards — idxstats for the read-level partition, featureCounts for per-gene matrices. Three host references carry gene models and produce matrices; the other three produce alignments only. The plant side is 50–160× the bacterial side by sequence, but the decisive factor is upstream of all of it: the read composition says these are polyA-selected libraries, which excludes bacterial mRNA by design and leaves only the plant-transcribed T-DNA behind on the bacterial reference.
